Zehn Minuten vor Mitternacht

New Year's Eve two thousand and thirty-five was cold and clear, minus six degrees, with a sky as full of stars as you rarely see in Berlin, because the city is usually too brightly lit. But that night, shortly before midnight, many people on Kastanienallee had already switched off their lights to see the fireworks better, so there were more stars above the courtyard of number thirty-one than Elif had ever seen in her life. She counted them until she gave up at a hundred and twelve. Under the bare chestnut tree a fire was burning in an old metal barrel that Andrei had brought from the scrapyard, and around the fire twenty people were standing or sitting on chairs in thick jackets, with hats and gloves, holding glasses of steaming mulled wine.

It was the first time both families had celebrated New Year's Eve together. Dan and Elena had come from Sibiu by car, two days' drive, with the boot full of honey, zacuscă (a vegetable spread), cozonac (sweet bread) and a bottle of țuică (plum brandy), which Dan, as he proudly told everyone, had declared at the border as “medicine for an old friend”. Sabine had come from Potsdam with a pot of potato salad, without which, as she said, no German New Year's Eve counts. And so the Romanian cozonac and the German potato salad now stood side by side on the table under the chestnut tree, and both mothers were watching very closely to see which would run out first. The cozonac won. Just.

Others had come too. Leo had the night off, for the first time in three New Year's Eves, and had come with Abena, his colleague from training, who was from Ghana and had never experienced a German New Year's Eve and flinched at every banger. Mara and Jakob were sitting with little Ingrid Hilde, who was stuffed into a thick winter snowsuit and was nothing but two big, lively eyes, in the warmest spot, right next to the fire. And even Dr Vogt was there, who that evening, exceptionally, didn't have a night shift and who, as he admitted to Lena with embarrassment, hadn't been awake at midnight for years without operating on someone. Elif had been given a notebook by Ludwig and the job of “taking the minutes”, in case anything important happened. She took the job very seriously and by half past ten already had two full pages, mostly about the potato salad.

Lena and Andrei had been engaged for a year and a half. Andrei had proposed to her in July two thousand and thirty-four in Sibiu, with the fifty-third carved bird, which held a gold ring with a little bee in its beak. Since then they had talked about the wedding again and again, and every time the discussion had got stuck at the same point: where. And yet they themselves had no firm opinion. The problem was the others. Elena wanted a church, a real, Orthodox one, with wedding crowns and candles, and Grandma Viorica, Dan's mother, who at ninety-two was no longer allowed to travel, in the front row. Sabine wanted Berlin, because Ludwig and Grete were here and because, as she put it, “half the family can't fly to Romania without being afraid for three weeks beforehand”. She meant Thomas.

Ludwig had watched the matter for long enough. That evening, at ten to twelve, he knocked three times on the metal barrel with his stick, so that it rang across the whole courtyard, and declared that, as the oldest member of the family and the owner of the house, he hereby called a family council. “We have ten minutes,” he said. “If we don't have a solution by midnight, the wedding's off and I'm keeping the ring.” Everyone laughed. But Ludwig was serious, at least about the ten minutes. In forty years at the BVG he had learned that people agree fastest when the tram is just about to leave.

Elena spoke first, in German, which she had been learning for four years and now spoke astonishingly well, with an accent Ludwig called “Transylvanian-charming”. She talked about Grandma, about the church in Sibiu where she and Dan had married, and Dan's parents before them, and about the crowns that are held above the heads of the bride and groom at an Orthodox wedding. “Without a church,” she said, “for us it's just a contract. Not a sacrament.” Sabine interrupted her, politely but firmly. She talked about Grete, who would turn a hundred in May if all went well, and about Ludwig, who was eighty-seven. “I understand you, Elena,” she said. “Really. Still, we also have two people here who can't travel. And one of them made this house what it is.”

Dan said nothing. At moments like these he tended to keep quiet and hand out honey, and that's what he did now: he went round with a jar of acacia honey and a spoon from one person to the next, and everyone got a spoonful, whether they wanted it or not. Hotte, who was of course there too, with his tram driver's cap and a woollen blanket on his knees, took two. Then he said, with his mouth full: “Don't get the problem. I married Erna twice. Once at the registry office, 'cause the state wanted it. And once in church, on the quiet, in nineteen seventy, 'cause her mum wanted it. And you know what? Each weddin' was nicer than the other.”

For a moment there was silence around the fire. Lena looked at Andrei, Andrei looked at Lena, and Elif, who was sitting between them on an upturned beer crate, looked at both of them and understood that something was happening right now that mustn't be missed. Because what Hotte had said was exactly what Lena and Andrei had been talking about secretly for weeks, in the evenings, on the first floor, when nobody was listening. Only they hadn't dared to say it out loud, for fear that both families would be offended that neither was getting the “real” wedding. “May I say something briefly about that?” asked Andrei. He stood up. “It is our wedding, after all.”

Then they explained, taking turns, as if they had rehearsed it without knowing they would need it today. In June, on a Saturday, the civil wedding in Pankow, in the same room where Mara and Jakob had got married, with Mrs Kranz as registrar, if she hadn't retired yet, and afterwards a party in the café and the courtyard, under the chestnut tree in bloom, with Grete in the front row, in her wheelchair, in her black hat with the feather. And in August, six weeks later, the church wedding in Sibiu, in the old church, with crowns and candles, with Grandma Viorica in the front row, on her own chair, which Dan would carry from home to the church. Two weddings. Two countries. Two grandmothers in the front row.

“If I may briefly sum up,” said Ludwig, looking at the watch Leo was holding up for him, “we have two weddings, two countries, two grandmothers in the front row and exactly three minutes left. Any objections?” Elena looked at Sabine. Sabine looked at Elena. It was a long look, the look of two mothers who had both won and both lost a little and who both knew it. Then Sabine said: “Just one. Who's paying for two weddings?” And Elena answered without hesitating, in German, with her Transylvanian accent: “Dan has honey. A great deal of honey.” And Dan, who hadn't understood a word, nodded seriously and handed round another round.

At midnight the sky above Berlin exploded. Rockets went up from everywhere, from the Mauerpark, from the TV tower, from the inner courtyards, and on Kastanienallee the church bells were ringing, and somewhere someone was playing the trumpet. Everyone in the courtyard clinked glasses, with mulled wine and țuică and champagne and, in Elif's case, hot cocoa, and everyone hugged, even people who had barely known each other an hour before. Elena hugged Sabine. Dan hugged Hotte, who protested, but not too loudly. Andrei lifted Lena up and spun her round in a circle until they almost both fell into the fire. And Ludwig stood a little apart, leaning on his stick, looking up at the coloured lights and thinking of Ingrid, as he did every year at midnight, only this time not sadly.

In the minutes, under the two pages about the potato salad, Elif wrote one last sentence, with cold fingers and in very big letters, because it was too dark to write small: “At midnight everyone laughed at once, in three languages. That was the end of the meeting.” Later, when Ludwig read the minutes, he said they were the best minutes he had ever read, and he had read plenty at the BVG.

On New Year's morning, while everyone was still asleep, Lena cycled to the care home. It was eight o'clock, the streets were full of scraps of paper from the fireworks and it smelled of gunpowder and snow. Grete was awake. Lately she was often awake early, Mrs Petersen said, as if she were afraid of missing something. Lena sat down by her bed and told her everything, about the family council, about Hotte, about the honey, about the two weddings. Grete listened with her eyes closed, and when Lena had finished, she opened them and asked a single question: “Which Saturday in June?” Lena said they didn't know yet. Grete nodded. “Then take an early one,” she said. “I intend to be there. But I also intend to turn a hundred in May. And both at once is a lot to ask, at my age.”

Lena rode back through the quiet, snowy streets, slowly, thinking about Grete's words. At home Andrei was already sitting in the kitchen, with coffee and the calendar from the bakery, which he had opened at the June page. He had had, as it turned out, the same idea. “Seventh of June,” he said, before she could say anything. “A Saturday. Three weeks after Grete's birthday. Early enough, but not too early.” Lena looked at the calendar. Something was already written on the seventh of June, in Andrei's neat engineer's handwriting: a little bird and next to it the word “yes”. Lena took a pen and wrote underneath, in her own handwriting: “yes”. Then she rang Mrs Kranz, who of course wasn't answering the phone on New Year's morning, and left her a message on the answering machine so long that the machine cut her off halfway through.
